newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Pork disease seen halting Taiwan stock bull run.
newsitem.headline: Pork disease seen halting Taiwan stock bull run.

text.p: News of a ban on exports of pork after an outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in Taiwan brought the stock market's bull run to a shuddering halt on Friday, but analysts said the outlook remains bullish.
The weighted index plunged 262.60 points, or 3.09 percent, to 8,230.07, the heaviest single-day loss in 11 months. Turnover was a frantic T$189.67 billion (US$6.9 billion).
"The market has not experienced such a sharp fall for a long time," said George Hou, a fund manager at Jardine Fleming. "It's time for a consolidation."
Brokers attributed Friday's huge decline to a government ban on exports of fresh and frozen pork after an outbreak of the contagious foot-and-mouth disease in the island's hog population.
Japan and South Korea on Friday also said they had banned pork imports from Taiwan indefinitely in the wake of the disease.
Not surprisingly, the food sector was hardest hit. It plummeted 5.9 percent, with most livestock shares tumbling the daily seven percent limit.
Analysts said the ban, which effectively cut off the island's pork export industry, would have a grave impact on relevant companies.
"Related food companies will be miserable for a while," Hou said.

Further dampening confidence was the government's latest bid to cool what it perceives as an overheated stock market and the central bank's persistent tighten of liquidity in the banking system, analysts said.
Securities and Exchange Commission head Lu Tung-ying sent a letter to the island's securities brokerages, urging them to protect investors' right after recent market rallies.
The letter was widely seen by analysts as an attempt to cool the stock fever.
"The hog foot-and-mouth disease is terrible. The SEC letter and the central bank tightening monetary policy are equally discouraging," said Tsao Chung-ping, an analyst for Ting Kong Securities.
Many experts have said the central bank's recent flurry of negotiable certificates of deposit issues was aimed at keeping a lid on the loose liquidity that has been fuelling the stock market rally.
"All this negative news will force the market to enter a correction phase," Tsao said.
Buoyed by what brokers called a liquidity-driven rally and a recovering economy, Taiwan's stock market is already one of the best performing markets in the world.
It has risen more than 20 percent in 1997 and 70 percent since a year ago, when rival China's intimidating war games and missile tests sent investors running for cover.
Many brokers said Friday's correction would probably be short lived.
"Investors are more cautious now and some may want to take a break. But they are by no means becoming bearish," said Lin Long-hsien of United Securities.
